speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head T of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This will be my focus for this speech.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While MND had all hands-on deck to better manage the delays in BTO construction through providing concessionary work passes for construction workers from neighbouring countries, to extending the duration of steel price protection to shield the construction companies from rising cost pressures, we were still unable to prevent the delay that is involved.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As I mentioned in my Budget speech, Singapore, as a small nation, we are very susceptible to supply chain disruptions and shocks.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With more unseasonable weather occurring globally and unstable political situations, the likelihood of these supply chain disruptions would only continue to persist.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Would MND be able to share the plans in place to build resilience in our construction ecosystem as we continue to be dependent on them as we develop this nation and manage the potential future disruptions?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Since the onset of hybrid working, many have realised that their existing homes may not be adequate to facilitate both working from home and for their children to continue home-based learning on certain school days.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Some may look to upgrade and having more space or the younger members of the family may choose to have their own spaces as they look out because they want to have a private working space.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Also, the trend may further pick up, as seen in some Western societies, whereby the young would leave their “nests” when they turn of age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: How can we prepare for this sociological change that we are seeing in our society today?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: At this point, I must commend MND for the timely intervention in the fast-heating property market in 2021.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As we all know, it is a tight balance to let market forces operate on its own to sustain a property market but, at the same time, introducing property cooling measures that do take some effect in the short term to prevent any possible housing bubbles.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But very often, we forget that, with limited land available, the affordability of public housing does hinge upon forward planning of land usage and allocation of land in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We need to ensure that we have a delicate balance in the many needs from residential, commercial, leisure and environmental sectors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In last year’s COS, MND announced the commencement of the public engagement exercise for the Long-Term Plan Review (LTPR).

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I personally attended some and am heartened to see the active participation of Singaporeans in envisioning, together with our land planners, on how they would like the future Singapore to be.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am encouraged at how our citizens have reflected the needs of incorporating natural and environmentally sustainable solutions in addressing housing needs moving forward.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But at the same time, they also acknowledged that, sometimes, trade-offs are inevitable.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: During my walkabouts and house visits, residents have expressed reasons why some choose to purchase public housing outside of the core central regions and they do prefer to have this in actually the mature estates.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I understand there could be some challenges because the mature estates are quite highly built by today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But their reasons do range from convenience of facilities in the mature housing estates to the ability to stay closer to their parents who can assist with caregiving for their young children and some also want to do the same for their elderly parents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As we pride ourselves for having one of the highest home ownerships around the world, we must continually find ways to enable this to remain affordable for the generations to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The use of the word "lottery" to refer to the allocation of HDB flats in the online domain dates to as far back as 2003.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The term "lottery effect" started coming into widespread use in 2015, after flats at The Pinnacle@Duxton reached their Minimum Occupation Period (MOP).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This lottery effect was explicitly commented on by Minister Lawrence Wong in 2016 when he was asked about it while he was the National Development Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He talked about possible measures to curb this effect and the PLH scheme was finally launched in 2021 with the project at Rochor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second PLH project was launched on 17 February, that is, last month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The PLH scheme continues to raise many questions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is it to avoid high prices for PLH flats, or is it to lower the lottery winnings of PLH flat owners?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If it is to avoid high price rises, that may not be the result of the subsidy clawback.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Six percent is likely to be included in a future sale price after the MOP, with a very long 89 years left on the lease.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Buyers and sellers are likely to simply add the 6% into their overall calculations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The unintended effect could be that prices are driven up even higher than they otherwise would be.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The higher the clawback, the higher the prices may be driven up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is not merely being asked to satisfy curiosity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the Minister makes known the criteria, then economists, urban planners and other experts may study the criteria and give feedback to the Government on their validity or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And the fourth question is: would the PLH scheme further drive up the prices of developments and resale flats close to PLH estates?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The scheme does not admit of gradual differences between PLH projects and non-PLH projects.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, I ask the Minister to share the calculations with this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These questions need answers, because it is important that the perceived solutions to problems do not create new problems themselves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ameliorating the lottery effect should not be a gamble.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, there are two main issues regarding the PLH model which I would like to address.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is that windfall gains or the so-called "lottery effect" from the PLH scheme is inadequately addressed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, my view is that the obvious outcome of this is that 6% will simply be factored into the asking price of the flats in the future – "priced in", in market lingo.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And if we are to use the example of The Pinnacle@Duxton, which frequently transacts for over a million dollars, this 6% will be less significant than the windfall gains the first-time seller of the PLH flat would stand to make.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, rather than having these onerous mechanisms, which distort the market, a simpler and more equitable solution, especially from the perspective of those who may not have the good fortune to buy into the new BTO PLH flats, who far outnumber the lucky few who managed to, is to reduce the quantum of subsidy given at the onset and provide higher subsidies for resale flat buyers who perhaps need them more.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Arguably, the widest subset of such HDB resale flats would have very high market values and would require significant additional subsidies to keep such flats affordable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Their need for additional subsidies is much more so than the still limited new launches of PLH flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And for many Singaporeans, the resale market is the only available housing option if they remain unsuccessful in the BTO lottery.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second issue is that singles are not being allowed to buy PLH flats even on the resale market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One of the most baffling aspects of the PLH model is its discrimination against singles, whereby singles are not allowed to buy PLH flats even on the resale market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As it stands, singles are not allowed to be sole owners of large BTO flats in mature estates and can only buy resale non-PLH flats if they are aged 35 and above.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, if there is no coherent reason why MND should impose additional restrictions on singles for PLH flats in the resale market, the message that this sends is that the needs, aspirations and sacrifices of singles are less valued, despite the Minister's claim that MND is not taking a step backward in this regard, as it would have the perception of doing so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the PLH model is new and will need to be reviewed over time, I had asked specifically in January this year if singles would, eventually, be allowed to be sole owners of new or resale PLH flats and, if this were to happen one day, what are the key considerations before these are lifted.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Minister Desmond Lee stated in January that the PLH model is designed with the objective of being inclusive for Singaporeans, and I trust that singles should be considered Singaporeans as well.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This has provided a lifeline for many of them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we can do more and help reduce the stress and uncertainty for single unweds who already feel that they are at the end of the road at times.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that single unwed parents can only get their rental flat after the child is born.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Assurance of having a roof over one’s head is as important as the roof.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Single unweds need a clear timeline for their applications to be completed so they have the assurance and can plan for the future.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most of us here would know the chaos of settling into a new home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us not forget that single unweds have to do so alone while caring for a newborn and with a median salary of only $600 a month.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A survey by Singapore’s Breastfeeding Mothers’ Support Group found that the top reason for stopping breastfeeding was the challenges of expressing milk at work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One thing working mothers say they need the most is a lactation room.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, buildings with a Gross Floor Area (GFA) of 10,000 square metres and above are required to only have at least one lactation room.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Expressing milk is not like using the toilet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unlike queuing up for a toilet which does not take that long, breastfeeding mothers are stuck when the only lactation room in the building is used.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some have shared that, out of desperation, they sometimes express milk in the storeroom or in the toilet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One mother shared: "HR arranged a janitor room which is so small and stuffy with no chair at all for me to express breast milk.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is so inconvenient as the janitor will need to go in and out all the time and I am always only able to express halfway through." Why subject breastfeeding mothers to such an unhygienic and undignified situation?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The HDB's web page lists seven separate priority schemes to book a flat under the Build-To-Order (BTO) or Sales of Balance Flat exercises.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My purpose in speaking on them today is to ask whether HDB has explored whether the thresholds of these priority schemes remain fit for purpose, in light of current demand in relation to supply, and under what circumstances does HDB review and adjust them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: While he explained that the numbers include repeat applications and that they increased partly due to the raising of the monthly income ceiling, he agreed that there is, currently, a strong demand for public housing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Taking into consideration this mismatch, the Government should take a look at whether the allocation of HDB flats, including through the use of these schemes, is being done in the fairest and most optimum way possible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: One thing that needs to be pointed out is that the priority schemes do not truly give priority.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: They do not ensure that applicants in the schemes get allocated flats over those not within the schemes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The schemes merely increase the probability of being allocated a flat and, thereby, give the appearance of being awarded priority.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If more than 30% of applicants are first-timer married couples with children, then there will be a ballot.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If a couple is unsuccessful, then they go into another balloting pool, but they could again be unsuccessful.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It must have happened many times in the past that non-prioritised applicants, for example, second-time applicants got BTO flats while perhaps so-called prioritised applicants did not.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Higher chances and multiple chances are just that – chances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It does not matter how many chances an applicant has over others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If they fail, it is still 0% success in getting a flat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If they are really deserving groups, the Government should look into the possibility of giving such groups actual priority.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The question, of course, is, who should get the priority and to what extent?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Should it remain at 30% for married couples with children, or should this go up to a higher percentage and include even newly-married couples?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This information would make it clearer to applicants and to market watchers what the current trends point to.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This would also prompt proactive adjustment of the policy scheme thresholds to be more attuned to the market and population demands.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To conclude, the current system is reminiscent of a previous system in allocating Primary school places.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Singaporeans were given priority in the sense that they got more ballot chances than Permanent Residents (PRs), but this meant that, many times, PRs would be successful while Singapore Citizens were not.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The principle is the same when it comes to BTOs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Government should consider making priority an actuality, rather than, for some – a probability.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, can I take the two cuts together?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: HDB indicated that it will help to match the applicants based on their common factors, to increase the likelihood of successful matches and reduce potential friction.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: How successful has this endeavour been and what is the percentage of flats allocated for JSS-OR?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: For those applying under the Family scheme, would HDB consider assigning larger rental flats to bigger families, such as those with more children, three-generation or extended family households?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Bigger units will reduce the problem of overcrowding and are more conducive for work-from-home (WFH) arrangements and for the children to study at home.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: I am also concerned that due to a lack of space, the children may choose to stay outside of the home more often.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This may lead to higher chances of them becoming wayward and delinquent and being victims of crimes; similarly, for the youths and adults who might be sleeping rough outside.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Their health and ability to study or work productively are also likely to be affected.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The average waiting time for a BTO project is four to five years, which is not a short period, especially for young couples with children on the way.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Many applicants have to stay with parents or other family members in the meantime.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This is a particularly challenging arrangement, with more people working from home these days.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Also, if HDB does not have sufficient units for PPHS, would HDB consider giving more grants to first-time owners for the purchase of resale flats, especially young families or singles?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This is in view of the higher prices of resale flats in recent transactions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: In particular, the bigger grants will be helpful to young couples desperate to find a resale flat to accommodate their growing families.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are many residents who have approached me to request assistance in appealing to HDB for subsidised rental housing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some have had to sell their flats after a divorce, or they have to move out of their current homes due to family issues.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most cannot afford to buy flats and face being homeless.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister said previously that the overall stock of rental flats is sufficient to meet demand.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, some residents exceed the Public Rental Scheme income threshold, but do not earn enough to afford to rent in the open market.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Others may be single unwed parents who do not qualify for the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, applicants who qualify for public rental housing may still have to wait between three and eight months before they can collect their keys.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many need a place to stay urgently as they do not have family or friends who can take them in.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How many approvals were granted under each scheme and what were the main reasons for approvals or rejections under these schemes?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I urge HDB to increase the number of flats under the IRH scheme.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: HDB could offer tiered rental rates that are higher than the Public Rental Scheme rates, but lower than the open market prices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will help many families and individuals that fail the strict means test of the current rental schemes, but are not earning enough to rent in the open market and need housing urgently, to avoid being left homeless.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, can I take the two cuts together?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Will there be more of such flats reserved to support first-timers and help them to settle down early?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry consider giving priority to those with children or with children on the way?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Will the Ministry be reviewing its existing scheme further to help encourage tenants to own their flats?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: As we think about our new way forward, I find it timely to bring up the Adjournment Motion that I moved last November on supporting diverse aspirations through rental housing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: If anything, I am glad that my views on how this policy will strengthen communities, as opposed to weakening them, have sparked conversations within and beyond this House from online discussions to forums and news articles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Perhaps, we could also explore expanding our notion of what it means to have homeownership via a rent-to-buy model.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: This scheme aims to ease the transition from renting to buying a home by providing subsidised rent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: This is not a new idea and, in fact, has been adopted in several parts of the world, such as the Rent to Own scheme in Wales or the Rent to Buy scheme in the UK.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: If home ownership is a cornerstone of this Government's housing policy, enabling residents the option to buy the same house after renting it for a certain number of years does seem like a viable solution.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: A solution might be for HDB to build more flats and allocate a portion of them as rent-to-buy units, instead of just limiting all rental flats to 1- or 2-room flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: This has the potential of concurrently addressing two systemic socioeconomic concerns of eliminating the stigma of residents living in rental flats and reducing the burden on the next generation of Singaporeans who could use their freed-up finances on housing to explore more daring career choices and/or entrepreneurial pursuits.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is especially so for elderly singles, some of whom are divorcees or estranged from their spouse or children.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For this group of people, due to their age and behaviour, they just cannot get along with another person in the same rental flat.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have come across cases where HDB pairs two total strangers to rent a 1-room flat.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, they are not able to get along with each other due to different habits, different hygiene practices or medical conditions.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As a result, sometimes, they quarrel with each other.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, one of them will move out and sleep at the void deck to avoid further quarrels.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What is the feedback on the scheme so far?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Were they able to stay with each other without quarrels?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What if a quarrel or dispute should break out between the two of them?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What if one of the applicants had an unacceptable behavioural issue, like hoarding?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would the operator try to mediate a settlement of the dispute or would the operator try to pair them with another single applicant?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, the prices of resale HDB flats have gone up quite a bit recently.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Such long waiting times are not just an inconvenience but seriously affect Singaporeans' life plans, such as causing young couples to delay starting a family.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The BTO demand and supply situation is made even more challenging by rising demands for BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: As the Minister recognised in January this year, a strong demand for flats has been driven by factors, including rising marriage and family formation rates, smaller household sizes and higher income ceiling, allowing more households to qualify.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: In view of these realities, it is an apt time for the Government to review and improve its approach towards the supply of HDB flats in order to keep waiting times in check.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: We recognise that large housing development projects simply take at least three to four years to complete.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Therefore, in order to achieve shorter average waiting times of, say, two to three years, Singaporeans must be allowed to apply for new flats at a point in time much closer to project completion and delivery.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: This basic idea is not new and, indeed, MND confirmed that, where possible, HDB has, since 2011, already been commencing some BTO projects ahead of demand or actual bookings.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: More recently, HDB also announced BTO flats with waiting times of two to three years, such as in Tenggah and Yishun.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Unfortunately, despite these apparent relaxations of the BTO system, average BTO wait times are still stubbornly long, suggesting that HDB's efforts, though welcomed, do not go far enough.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: In order to maintain parity between the two tracks and to mitigate the risk of vacant flats, the express lane option should perhaps offer applicants less specificity in their preferences.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: For example, an applicant may only specify a unit type in the ranking of different floors of the zones.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: For this to work, there may need to be a larger percentage of HDB stock being contracted every year ahead of demand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: To be clear, this is not a proposal to revert to the pre-BTO era with the registration for flats system.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: We saw an oversupply of flats in the wake of the Asian Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: However, the proposal does involve an acceptance of some risk of excess supply if there were to be a severe demand shock.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: That being said, I strongly believe that such a risk is low and, in any event, worth taking, given the stubborn problem of long BTO wait times plaguing us today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: It is worth pointing out that, since 2010, BTO flats have consistently been multiple times oversubscribed, with only one exercise where the ratio specific to that of 2-room Flexi Flats was close to one time.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, there were HDB flats built in advance in the past and allocated successfully.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: I hope that more BTOs could be built in the Sengkang and Punggol new towns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: According to the latest Government census, the proportion of singles has risen across age groups.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The increase was most significant for those between 25 and 34 years of age.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Similarly, the proportion of singles among those aged 30 to 34 rose to 41.9% for males and 32.8% for females.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In 2018, then Minister for National Development Lawrence Wong stated in Parliament that as marriage rates among singles under 35 was still high, the age of 35 remained a valid number.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Does the Government intend to move from 35 as the magic number?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: There is a prevailing orthodoxy that Singaporeans should be married by 35 and that offering flats to those of a younger age could somehow discourage marriage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Alternately, there may be an assumption that offering flats to those younger than 35 would jeopardise the value of filial piety.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The National Youth Council's 2021 publication on the state of youths in Singapore is helpful in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The publication reports the results of the National Youth Survey 2019 covering those between 15 and 34 years of age.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Those surveyed were asked: how important are the following aspirations or life goals in your life?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: They were given 19 possible choices to rank from not important at all to very important.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Both choices were ranked somewhat important or very important by at least 95% of the respondents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To our youths, filial piety and having one's own home are not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Indeed, they are both almost equally important values.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To be clear, strong family relationships did not automatically mean marriage or having children to those surveyed because those were the 10th and 11th choices respectively.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: One assumption we should question is that offering flats to 28-year-olds would discourage genuine interest in long-term marriage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Is it not possible that some people who want to be married may be discouraged from tying the knot early because they prefer to have financial security before getting hitched and having children?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If a single person is allowed to purchase HDB property, whether BTO or resale, earlier, this may well open new prospects to, concomitantly, move on to marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In addition, the prospect of purchasing a flat at 28 years of age, down from 35, would leave more scope for the growth of one's CPF balances for peace of mind and for retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We must ask whether it is reasonable to continue disallowing singles from purchasing a BTO or resale flat once they are financially able to do so before 35.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, can I take the two cuts together?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This is viable, provided that the buyers are able to keep their jobs and maintain uninterrupted employment.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: I spoke about this during the debate on the President's Address in September 2020.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The employment situation today is less favourable for holding long mortgage tenures, compared to the past when people used to hold jobs for life.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Going forward, people will change jobs more frequently and quite a number are making a living from the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This new job trend and the higher macroeconomic risk backdrop should be captured in the analysis of the affordability of HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This would also provide flexibility to structure lower instalment payments by stretching the loan tenure should financial circumstances of the buyer change over time.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Alternatively, HDB should find ways to increase affordability, such as giving more grants, to help first-time owners with their BTO flats, especially those from the lower-income group.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: HDB should continue to tap on technology and improve building techniques to keep the cost of construction of BTO flats low, as it confronts rising labour and material costs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Ministry share what measures HDB is implementing to improve affordability of its BTO flats?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Some owners have difficulty selling their flats due to the Ethnic Integration Policy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: They are mostly from the minority ethnic groups.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: A few owners had complained that they could not even get a single offer to negotiate upon.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This situation causes hardship for families who need to move for personal reasons, such as those that need to be nearer other family members who can be caregivers, or who need money for retirement or family emergencies and, hence, are downgrading.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Will HDB consider helping them out and facilitate such sales by providing a grant or subsidy to a buyer from the eligible minority group?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This will help to plug the difference between the sellers' asking price and what the eligible buyer can afford.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This grant can be piloted in areas where there are more mismatches and where the gaps are more significant.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Alternatively, HDB can act as a buyer of last resort for such flats and purchase the flats from the sellers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: These flats can then be leased to singles or families in the eligible minority ethnic groups under the parenthood provisional housing scheme or public rental scheme.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Similarly, BTO and sale of balance flats, which have been reserved for certain ethnic groups under the EIP and which have remained unsold for an extended period of time can be included under PPHS and the public rental scheme.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Some of them wanted to sell and right-size their flat because their children have moved out.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Some wanted to sell their flat because they needed a larger flat due to increased family members.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: However, due to EIP, they are unable to sell their flat to a Chinese family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: A few of them wrote to me to say that they have advertised for several months without receiving a single offer from someone of the minority race.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Some of the potential buyers for their flat know of the policy and they may depress the prices because they know that there is limited demand for these flats due to the restriction.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: However, it seems unfair that existing minority sellers of the flat have to carry the burden of having to accept a lower price for their flat due to a national policy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This is especially so if he has not been able to sell the flat for several months due to EIP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In September last year, I asked the Minister for National Development a written Parliamentary Question for data on each of the respective five-yearly intervals from December 1990 to December 2020 to detail, amongst other things, the names of the EIP-affected neighbourhoods where at least one EIP limit was reached and the total number of HDB units in each of these aforesaid neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Ministry only provided data for 1990 and 2020, even though it was able to provide information at five-yearly intervals for the EIP-related question earlier.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Why was it unable to provide the information as requested?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, the fact that Singaporeans of various races live and interact with one another in harmony differentiates us from many other countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Similar to three other Members who have shared on the EIP, the unintended economic consequences of EIP have been repeated frequently, including in this House.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Minorities sometimes face or perceive difficulties in selling their HDB flats at their desired price, especially where they are prevented from selling to Chinese buyers who make up a large proportion of the market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have also heard the same from my Malay and Indian residents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we move to unite larger neighbourhoods with community hubs like Our Tampines Hub and Kampung Admiralty, is it possible to loosen the block-by-block quota and enforce a second-level "cluster" or "district" quota, while still maintaining the broad principles in EIP?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, peace and quiet are two of the most important characteristics of a better living environment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All residents, whether they are staying in HDB or private properties, should have the right to peace and quiet in order to catch up on their rest and sleep.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, for some beleaguered residents of HDB blocks with sky or roof gardens, they have not been able to enjoy this basic right for years.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We require more regular patrols by the authorities and agencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I want to take this opportunity to thank the Safe Distance Enforcement Officers, the Police, MOM, NEA, HDB, the Town Councils, RC volunteers and residents for all their efforts in patrolling the sky gardens, tackling safe distance breaches, noise disturbances and disamenities over the years.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many residents have sent me emails to thank our volunteers and agencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will greatly cut down on the requirements on manpower.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As these sky gardens will increasingly be a common feature in future public housing developments, I appeal to the Ministry to reconsider installing a gate to such sky gardens as the longer-term solution.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The price of materials has shot up, wages have increased and the cost of bringing in foreign workers is also elevated.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The construction industry's confidence has been shaken up late, resulting in shorter payment terms and demands for higher upfront payments.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Yet, HDB's grants to Town Councils have not kept up with these price increases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Some may suggest that Town Council's existing funds can be used to cover the cost increases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: However, doing so would be unfair to the majority of residents as each project mainly benefits residents living in a particular precinct.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It is also unfair for residents of those precincts if the new projects are pared down to meet the original budget.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Second, can HDB provide contractors and subcontractors for town improvement projects some price protection for raw materials, like steel and concrete – similar to that of HDB's BTO projects?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This will better ensure residents receive comparable amenities, regardless of market conditions at the time of tendering.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And third, can the Ministry explore more measures to restore confidence among construction firms, so as to ameliorate the need for onerous upfront payment terms?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This could also help temper price increases across the industry.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, a fairer, greener, and more inclusive Singapore requires fairer, greener and more inclusive housing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fairer: while the EIP continues to be relevant, it remains a concern that it causes negative externalities to minority home owners who face difficulties in selling their flats as well as renters and home buyers who cannot get a flat close to their parents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can the Minister address the rough edges of the policy?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Greener: buildings account for a large share of emissions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister share how HDB is playing its part to move to greener buildings, both new builds and retrofits?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: More inclusive: can the Minister update on the outcomes of the policy to integrate rental units with purchased units instead of dedicated rental blocks?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What more can be done to facilitate the forming of support networks within the community for rental flat residents in these integrated blocks?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister also update on measures to enhance the HDB experience for the elderly and persons with disability?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Miss Rachel Ong, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A citizen's contribution to the nation-building effort is not limited by their marital status.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Singles and married citizens can both participate in the workforce and serve the community.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It may be argued that singles could even expend more time at work and the community than those with family commitments.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, while singles may not have to care for children, many provide essential care for ageing family members, be it physically, through financial support, or both.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: My residents, who are single, have shared that in the bid to prioritise housing for families, they feel that the housing and home ownership policies are less equitable for singles.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Such a housing policy impacts not only space allocation, but cumulative asset value over time for singles.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With that said, how can HDB housing subsidies be made more equitable across both single and married Singapore Citizens who contribute to Singapore's nation-building efforts in their different ways?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I believe that the mandate to keep our housing affordable to Singapore Citizens extends to all Government-built flats, not only BTOs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Apart from the new flats under the Prime Land Housing model, are there plans for MND to regulate the prices of the HDB resale market to make housing more accessible to Singapore Citizens who do not qualify for the BTO market?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan; you may take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, heartland shops are a precious part of our HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They provide convenience to residents by bringing various goods and services close to homes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They provide jobs and livelihoods in the community.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Heartland shop proprietors are quite often also residents within the same estate and they hire assistants, roles quite often filled by residents who are caregivers or seniors, who need or value work flexibility and proximity to home.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And heartland shops provide a place for residents to meet one another, for ties to form, a focal point for each community.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In short, heartland shops make our HDB estates not only places to live, but also work, play and bond.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, many forces are disrupting the retail sector at large.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And heartland shops, too, would need to keep abreast with changes, transform where they must, and indeed, look beyond the estate to capture new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To this end, how does MND plan to support heartland shops to thrive and remain a vibrant part of our HDB estates?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Could MND update on its plans to formalise such a framework to require heritage studies for certain sites?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, since MND and MOH launched their assisted living pilot, the Community Care Apartments last year, there has been a lot of interest by seniors – seniors who wish to right-size, live independently, with the right care support when needed, and in the company of fellow seniors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I have asked before in this House, and I would like to ask again, if MND plans to launch more of such Community Care Apartments?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And would MND be minded to work with the private sector, to promote the development of private assisted living options?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our high housing density, in both the HDB and private estates, affords Singapore the chance to create excellent age-in-place conditions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We can create a strong eco-system of well-integrated, affordable and high-quality private assisted-living and home-based healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is an issue that many of my colleagues and I from PAP care deeply about.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We do so because we believe that doing so will help our seniors and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Doing so will minimise the cost associated with ageing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To create this ecosystem, we must create a strong vision, build common physical infrastructure, provide a digitalised services platform and create a suitable financing framework, as well as to put in place effective regulations and standards.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Does MND have plans to guide or promote the development of private assisted living options for residents staying in both the HDB and private estates?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many seniors wish to right-size while retaining their independence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Single or widowed seniors, especially those with no children, often do not have anyone to turn to for housing advice and one bad decision could spiral into another.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What efforts and safeguards are in place to ensure that seniors understand their various options and financial ability in considering housing options, prior to making a firm decision?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given the high demand, how can these Community Care Apartments be complemented by programming on the ground?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given rising housing prices and competing uses for land, does MND have a framework in place to keep the price of these homes at an affordable level for our seniors?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore’s Public Rental Scheme (PRS) is a key social safety net for households with no other housing options or family support.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of these families aspire to move on to home ownership, especially those young families with working-age adults.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, some families have previously owned an HDB flat but fallen on hard times, such that HDB subsidies are less readily available.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Others receive variable incomes in the gig economy, making it more difficult for them to access loans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And for those who are unable to, what are the typical barriers which prevent them from doing so?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During COVID-19, we saw an increasing number of PRS applicants who may not fall within the original policy intent but do have pressing needs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given limited resources, does MND have plans to expand or evolve the options, criteria and objectives of the PRS to cater to a more diverse group of Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Singapore continues to develop, we have seen how our heritage districts have evolved over the years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are an important part of keeping our history and traditions alive and relevant today.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But our local businesses in these districts have faced many challenges in the last few years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What plans does the Government have to reinvigorate the vibrancy of Kampong Glam and our other heritage districts after the pandemic shock to increase footfall?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government consider looking into best practices on tenant mix to ensure a seamless integration of our older tenants and newer stallholders in the area?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What plans does the Government have to balance heritage and conservation against the risk of gentrification and how does the Government intend to involve all the local stakeholders?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The EPE studies the ecological profile of green spaces in Singapore and understands how these spaces can boost ecological connectivity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One year on from its launch, what are EPE’s findings so far?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How have findings from EPE shaped NParks’ internal nature conservation strategies and approaches to safeguarding our green spaces?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, it has been two years since MND announced its City in Nature vision.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: May we please have an update on the progress made on transforming Singapore into a City in Nature and how NParks will continue ramping up efforts on this front?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: What more can be done to inform and interest our people, especially the young, in conserving our biodiversity and nature?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Chairman, COVID-19 has posed significant challenges to the construction industry over the last two years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The industry appreciates the tremendous support that MND has provided since the start of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: With the Omicron variant, the construction industry continues to face challenges.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can MND provide an update on the help provided to the construction industry thus far, especially on the progress of replenishing the sector's foreign manpower, the availability of bank financing, especially for subcontractors, as well as MND's current assessment of where the sector is heading?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can MND also share on how the Government can, together with the various built sector trade associations and chambers, continue to help our industry overcome the challenges from COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: COVID-19 has highlighted the pressing need to reduce our reliance on low-skilled foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: At the same time, digitisation and automation can significantly help us transform our industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: For example, digitisation allows players to better coordinate and, therefore, increasing efficiency.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The automation of construction techniques also promotes the use of technology on site, as well as the pre-fabrication and modularisation of construction methodologies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: More importantly, digitisation and automation may create jobs that appeal to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can MND share on the measures that the Government will take to build a more resilient and manpower-lean built sector, as well as to encourage further localisation of jobs in the sector?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, prefabricated prefinished volumetric construction (PPVC) is attractive as it has been assessed to improve building productivity by up to 40%, resulting in substantial onsite manpower and time savings.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is green and sustainable since it reduces construction material wastage and can incorporate green features, such as green concrete.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is popular because it reduces all the disamenities of a construction environment, such as noise and dust.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would MND provide an update on the status of PPVC adoption in all categories of construction, including for HDB projects?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Why is it required only for these selected sites?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would MND consider requiring more builders to use PPVC and speed up its adoption?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: What are the constraints which are preventing wider adoption?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With technology and advancement, new buildings today can use green material and smarter designs to reduce emissions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But in a highly built‐up environment like Singapore, we have many mature estates with a high concentration of buildings that are decades old.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many of these buildings are homes to our people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, how will the Government and BCA continue to support our transition into a low‐carbon built environment?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What are our progress and quick wins so far?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How can emissions in existing buildings be reduced without affecting homes, where precious memories are forged?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The quantum advancement in green technology and digitalisation of energy can allow us to move from reactive to predictive maintenance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These can reduce waste, save energy and enhance user experience.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over the long term, these can lead to cost savings for the public, too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could the Government give an update on its plans to leverage smart technology and data to enhance the quality of living while preserving the tangible and intangible values of housing estates?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While this may provide an option, shifting can be a more complicated decision for many, more than one would imagine, especially if the residents have been living in the same flat for a considerable time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some prefer to stay on, even if it meant carrying their elderly relative on their back, or together with the relative's wheelchair, down two flights of stairs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But a year on, residents in affected blocks have continued to speak to me of their frustration with no same floor lift access.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Unsurprisingly, the Lift Access Housing Grant is no panacea to many of the residents who spoke to me.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many residents feel frustrated by HDB's explanation of the issue of costs, something which could have been avoided if HDB had tendered out lift upgrading projects consisting of these blocks with design issues together with the bulk of the HDB blocks with no design issue for LUP access to all residents in the blocks, as former Hougang Member of Parliament Png Eng Huat had raised in the House way back in 2014.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also hope that HDB will work on this issue expeditiously to bring lift upgrading to all.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.30 pm until 3.50 pm.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Today, we are at the intersection of urbanisation, digitalisation and innovation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: By not enabling smart facilities through technology, they will face even more challenges ahead by not knowing where to harness efficiencies using conventional FM methods.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: There is enough technology in this space to allow for some upgrades through incorporating IOT solutions to better harness and understand the environment and know which part of the facilities to manage and be more effective in the waterflow.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Below are a few areas for consideration in the transformation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: First, use of data analytics to improve maintenance outcomes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Second, share best practices in design or retrofits that enable optimal building performance and sustainability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Third, focus on outcome-based contracts to achieve cost efficiency and improve the service delivery.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Lastly, partner industry players to map technology solutions and invest in R&D for complex infrastructure environment analysis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Minister Desmond Lee replied to me previously that MND does not intend to play a cat-and-mouse game on this issue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Indeed, let us stop chasing each other and let us focus on the facts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: He gave a breakdown on the four reasons HDB bans cats. "Reason 1: 'Cats are generally difficult to contain within the flat'.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: So are dogs, birds, mice and even humans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Reason 3: 'Cats tend to defecate or urinate in public areas'.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And dogs bark, especially at strangers walking past a flat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Birds, especially parrots, make a lot of noise, too.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: My residents in Bedok Reservoir and Hougang have given me feedback on the nuisance caused by pigeons, crows, mynahs and even quails around the housing estates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The proliferation of the bird population is often a public hygiene concern and, in the case of crows, a safety issue, which worries residents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Aljunied-Hougang Town Council (AHTC) has been doing its part to combat this problem.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The AHTC puts up banners to caution residents against bird feeding and works with residents to identify and report feeders.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It advises food stall operators on proper food waste disposal methods and our conservancy workers regularly remove unattended food sources.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Town Council also conducts regular tree pruning and, as a last resort, pigeon culling.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Despite these efforts, the bird nuisance problem has persisted.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: NParks, occasionally, sets up crow traps but these are rather ineffective as crows are intelligent creatures and tend not to fall for these traps.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I believe this problem is not unique to AHTC.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: These may include more public education to discourage bird feeding, setting up CCTV monitoring and stepping up enforcement action against bird feeders.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It would be helpful if NParks could regularly share with Town Councils its research and recommendations on best practices for controlling the population of various bird species.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It could step up efforts to trap and relocate birds in areas where they are causing a nuisance to the public.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Together with the efforts of Town Councils, MND's stepped up involvement could help residents and our ardent friends to co-exist more peacefully in our urban environment.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Miss Cheryl Chan, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The OneService App began as a one-stop platform for Singaporeans to provide feedback on municipal issues without having to go through hoops to figure out the appropriate agency to undertake the issue raised.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Since 2015, it has, indeed, brought much operational efficiencies to both the Government agencies and Singaporeans alike.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: What has the adoption rate been like for these new features?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Can the Minister also share if there are any additional features that are still under consideration and yet to be implemented?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: How does MSO envisage the future of the OneService App?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Since the start of the pandemic, many people have experienced working from home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Even as the borders are gradually opened up and corporations transition to hybrid work, this trend of hybrid working is likely to stay post-pandemic.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: While some relish the prospect of spending more time with their loved ones, there are also more media reports and ground feedback on neighbourly disputes as a result of spending more time at home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: But there is also difficulty underlying mediation, as when the relationship is acrimonious, this option may be futile.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: For the longstanding and intractable cases, what else can be done if the cases taken through the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals (CDRTs) still remained inconclusive?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I have had such case feedback, some of which occur in private condominiums where the MCST and the by-laws are unable to assist.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Will MSO consider having other pilot schemes, like Project Restore, that is run by social service agency, the Lutheran Community Care Services (LCCS).

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: LCCS actually gets parties to come together and talk and they create what they call a "peace-making circle".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The parties can discuss issues objectively and without feeling being judged.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: And since the function is targeted at the vulnerable groups, will MSO consider a more extensive outreach effort to educate the mentioned group on the use of the app and how to maximise its usage?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A resident can submit feedback but there is no information about the status of operational processes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sometimes, the case is closed before the problem is officially resolved, something that Member Cheryl Chan has earlier raised as well.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does smart technology assist us in this area?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Another area is the resolution of neighbourly disputes, such as community noise and corridor obstruction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such issues have been aggravated by work from home arrangements during the pandemic period.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I think it was useful for OneService to disclose the units in the resident's block which are undergoing renovation works so that, in the event of noise issues, the resident can contact the owners of the unit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, if the flat owner has downloaded the app, they would be able to see the concerns and respond, with a mediator on-hand to assist.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some residents do not wish to attend in-person mediation at the Community Mediation Centre or bring the matter to CDRT.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Technology has made online mediation more accessible and popular.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As our population ages, we should aspire towards having our housing typology cater to our life needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially so when there is a growing preference among our seniors to age in place.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Good housing designs should adopt universal design elements that are not only elderly-friendly but also cater to impaired mobility due to unexpected illness, injury or disability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Enhancement for Active Seniors (EASE) is a good initiative.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But sometimes, residents wait until something has happened, like after a fall, before they make the application.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should take a more proactive approach towards home safety for the elderly because a fall can really impair them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Indeed, we must do more, beyond the basic infrastructure, something that the PAP Seniors Group is pushing for.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What other upcoming senior-friendly initiatives will be introduced to our housing estates?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How is MND working with MSF and MOH to ensure that our built environment supports ageing in place?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: COVID-19 has exacerbated the challenges in municipal service delivery, with manpower constraints even more binding, especially over the past two years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Because more Singaporeans are working from home, we see a significant increase in the use of common area within our estates as well as increased disputes among neighbours.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: We also see heightened expectations from our residents with regard to cleanliness standards.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: With our Government's digitalisation effort, Singaporeans also expect timely and comprehensive responses from MSO's app.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: All these conditions create considerable challenges for MSO despite all the hard work and resources that MSO has already committed to keeping our estates clean.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Many times, it is about heavy steps from the higher floors, noise from shifting of tables, chairs or furniture in the middle of the night.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Sometimes, it is about noisy music or children screaming.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Due to unhappiness about the noise, neighbours do start quarrelling with one another and allegations are made.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Sometimes, abusive language is also used against one another and the living environment in the area becomes hostile.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: It seems that we are helpless to help these neighbours resolve such disputes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The resident has to simply live with the noise.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Last year, I spoke about the disputes between neighbours during the Committee of Supply (COS) debate for MinLaw.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: I asked how CDRT could help to resolve these disputes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: However, surely, a better option is to try to nip the problem in the bud before it even gets to CDRT.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Is there room for Government agencies to do more to address such neighbourly disputes?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Can we do more to promote neighbourliness among residents so that they can build on the relationship with one another and become friends who can discuss issues without having to resort to loud voices against each other or to quarrel?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Can such disputes be resolved by encouraging neighbours to be more considerate towards one another?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I was staying at my first matrimonial flat, a 3-room resale flat in Toa Payoh.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It was a slab block design where the units are side by side and have windows that open into the common corridor.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We had some friends over for a gathering and it lasted into the wee hours.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: On hindsight, we must have sounded especially loud in the quiet of the night.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Our next-door neighbour, an elderly uncle, approached us at around 2.00 am, complaining about the noise and reminding us to keep our volume low.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We felt so bad, we bought some chicken essence to express our apology and wished him well.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: After that episode, we became more careful and managed to maintain a friendly relationship with the uncle for the rest of our stay there.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Personally, I feel that such matters are best settled between neighbours.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: If he had reported to the authorities immediately, I could conclude that he preferred a more officious approach towards our relations.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: On the other hand, if he had suffered in silence, I would not have known that it was an issue and might have organised even more house parties.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: His frustrations and unhappiness would have built up without me knowing.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We should not let the first encounter to be an unpleasant one.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Typically, a neighbourly dispute is more complicated, with different versions of the situation.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The misunderstanding and mistrust between neighbours are likely to have developed over years.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Having said that, there will be cases when there is ill will or neighbours who are just being difficult and unreasonable.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I will explain how we at MND are doing this in these key priority areas: (a) keeping public housing affordable and accessible and meeting the housing aspirations of Singaporeans; (b) transforming the way we design, build and maintain our city; (c) growing our City in Nature; and (d) safeguarding our built heritage.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: My MND colleagues will give more details on the various areas of our work.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Helping Singaporeans own their homes is a key national priority and a promise that the Government has been committed to for decades.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: A home that we can call our own provides the basic foundation to raise our families and bring up our children.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If you look at other cities, they have different ways of housing their people.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Some leave housing largely to the private market while others provide rental flats to certain demographic groups at subsidised rates.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are committed to ensuring that public housing remains affordable and accessible to help meet the housing aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We plan the supply of new flats by taking into account long-term factors, such as demographic changes and trends, including family formation rates and household sizes.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We also monitor the market and make adjustments to meet cyclical shifts in demand.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In addition, we provide generous grants for first-timers, for both new and resale flat purchases, with more help for lower-income buyers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked if we should review our affordability benchmarks.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Most first-timers buying HDB flats in the non-mature estates only need to set aside a quarter of their income or less to pay for their monthly loan instalments.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is already significantly lower than the international benchmark of between 30% and 35% for affordable housing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And it allows buyers to pay their mortgage with their CPF savings, with little or no cash outlay.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To ensure prudent use of public funds, we impose a monthly income ceiling to allocate housing subsidies to those who may need it more.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The income ceiling for executive condominiums (ECs) is even higher, at $16,000.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Households earning an income above $14,000 have a variety of housing options, such as resale flats, ECs and private developments.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The income ceilings were just raised in 2019, but we will continue to review them.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the immediate term, the pandemic has had a serious impact on the construction sector, causing housing delays, concerns about the tight housing supply and worries about rising resale home prices.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At the same time, marriage and family formation, a growing trend of smaller households and the current low interest rate environment have led to strong housing demand in both the BTO and resale markets.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is difficult work, especially in the midst of an ongoing pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our HDB colleagues have been on the ground, working closely with contractors to overcome the many challenges that COVID-19 has thrown at them: (a) bringing in workers safely to make up for manpower shortages due to border restrictions; (b) coping with the impact of public health measures on productivity at worksites; (c) sharing cost increases when prices of construction materials rose sharply; (d) localising more precast production and stockpiling more materials in case of further disruptions in supply chains and so on.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are also increasing the supply of private housing through the Government Land Sales Programme and, last year, we introduced measures to cool the property markets to pre-emptively address the risk of home prices running ahead of market fundamentals and, in doing so, keep housing affordable for genuine home buyers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, that is how we are addressing the housing situation today – by increasing both private and public supply to meet the strong demand while moderating market movements and minimising delays.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are not out of the woods yet, because the pandemic situation remains uncertain and the geopolitical situation increasingly volatile.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But the delays have impacted many Singaporeans’ life plans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We seek your understanding and support, as we press on to try to minimise delays and deliver your homes to you as soon as we can.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the meantime, for first-timer families who face challenges renting on the open market, we assist them with interim rental housing under the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS).

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have tripled the number of PPHS flats offered at each application exercise.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, we are prioritising families with the greatest needs.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That said, around half of the applicants who are invited to select a flat decide not to do so, suggesting that many may have other options.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: HDB also offers Interim Rental Housing (IRH) on a case-by-case basis to those who do not have other interim housing options.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To Mr Gerald Giam’s suggestion, the supply of IRH flats varies to meet the demand, as these flats are also used for PPHS or public rental.
